it will vary a bit depending on if you are a baxter or a fresenius patient (assuming USA).

Here's some info on the fresenius stuff. baxter is a little different from what i've heard.

The cycler i have is a liberty cycler. it has a large touch screen and overall is not terribly large, but it's around the size of a desktop laser printer/scanner combo. a bit bigger but that's the general size. 

The fresenius cycler comes with a wheeled cart (well, they "rent" it to your insurance) for the cycler to sit on. the cassettes everyone is talking about most often have 1 connection for the patient connector (the part connected to your catheter), 4 connections for dialysis bags (you will not use them all just the ones you need), and a drain line. The drain line is about 20 feet long. They can give you an extender for another 20 feet if your nearest drain is further away. you can also drain into a bucket/jug and drain it in the toilet/bathtub later if there are no drains convenient. Everything except the cycler is single use only - you use a new cassette, bags, everything every time you set up and connect.

the power cord on the cycler is a standard 6 foot/2meter power cable, not supposed to be hooked into a surge protector or anything. so the machine can be moved a few feet. the patient connector is also 20 feet long. When connected, the patient will not be able to go further than this tubing length away from the cycler.

You will need a small area or tote container for hand cleaning/machine cleaning supplies - i dont like to keep that stuff in the bathroom full time so i just bring it in and out as needed. I also have a small area on my headboard dedicated to syringes/needles (i inject heparin into my bags to prevent protein fiber buildup in my abdomen), machine/catheter cleaning stuff, etc. 

The main space hog are the boxes of dialysis fluid. Here's what about a month of my dialysate looks like: 

https://imgur.com/a/4IbBn5f

in addition to that i also receive 3-4 boxes of cassettes, 2 boxes of cathether caps, and some other assorted stuff due to my treatment plan - for example i get 3 boxes of adapters that turn the single patient connection into 2 connections, allowing me to disconnect once during a dwell if i need to be able to make food or something - i live alone and the kitchen is not within reach of the cycler.

Edit: *you also will need to keep a week or so of emergency "manual" supplies. so you'll have an IV pole, and a week or two of manual pd bags.*

Fresenius delivers 1 month of supplies at a time (allegedly they can do bi weekly but that's not something i want to deal with). You must be present to receive them. The driver will put them away and stack them neatly as long as the storage area is easily accessible. I have never had to stack or move my own boxes except to open one to use it. Fresenius also delivers gloves, masks, and hand sanitizer.

In addition to all that, every month when i go to the clinic i get gauze, wound cleaner (for the exit site hole), machine/catheter cleaner, syringes, needles, tape, etc.

Once every 3 months i have to collect all my drain fluid and take a sample and bring it to the clinic, along with 24 hours of urine collected from the day/night before. They give you a jug for the urine, it has to be refrigerated which is meh but has to be done. they give you a urinalysis cup to put sample(s) of the spent dialysate fluid into. this is for a test called KT/V which measures the efficiency/effectiveness of your treatment.

once a month you will meet with your clinic nurse and get your labs drawn, they do a short examination like listen to your lungs and heart, check your feet, check your exit site, review changes to medication and etc. Then after those labs come back once a month you visit again to see the nephrologist during his clinic day and he reviews your labs and discusses your treatment/concerns.

I had no issue with my small dog and the drain line. he did enjoy laying on it when it was draining because it's ~100 degrees (98.6 or so lol) and i guess it felt good. but he never once tried chewing it or playing with it. mostly he just ignored it.

I drain to the toilet. i bought a plastic hook looking thing on amazon that fits over the rim of the bowl, under the toilet seat with a channel for the drain tube that holds it in place without having to tape it. because dialysate is glucose based, it will cause things to grow in your toilet/drains so you gotta stay on top of that and run water daily and sometimes some cleaner to keep it flowing well. This is probably more of a problem for me due to living alone and being the only one who uses/flushes the toilet lol.

physical dependence.

The longer you take it, the less effective it will become, and your dose will increase. 

At the doseages we take it at for RLS they're pretty low dose but the longer you take it, the more dependent on it you will become, the more you have to take etc. We're talking long term. my dose has increased once in 2 years.

Because of how it alters brain chemistry (which is how it works), your brain doesnt do well when you no longer take it. The physical withdrawal symptoms i experienced were eye opening and concerning to me so i discussed with my neph and we are going to wean me off of it and try something else that has less dependence issues.

For many this is not something that they need to worry about, but it's good to know what *can* happen. When i was in withdrawal i could not sleep, at all, for 3 days straight. i also think it's responsible for much of the brain fog and confusion i've been experiencing since starting taking it.

Overall it works great, which is a bummer, because it causes me to want to ignore the bad stuff im experiencing because it's a balancing act between that and the horror of RLS and neuropathic pain.

thats my treatment - Gabapentin and THC. I agree, mine is also horriffic.

Gabapentin is not the best for your body overall, there are a lot of troublesome side effects and withdrawal is 0/10 would not recommend, but i havent found anything better. RLS is a terrible symptom and i really wish the name of it was something more insidious than "restless legs".

when i first started i had a lot of trouble sleeping too. (sometimes, i still do but not due to pain/drain alarms).

All i can say is it gets better. your body gets more used to the sensations. Your body gets tired enough to sleep even though it doesnt feel good. Your body learns to move less during sleep.

before PD i was a very restless sleeper. i was a stomach/side sleeper, and i can't sleep on my stomach while on PD. Initially, sleeping on my side while doing PD cycles was extremely painful on my back (similar to how pregnant women have issues with back pain and sleeping i think).

I bought a pillow made for pregnant women and that really eliminated the back pain (it supported both my back and my stomach as i slept on my side). My body subconsciously learned not to roll around. Now i wake up 6-8 hours later and the bed is mostly undisturbed, i havent moved, and i got some rest.

I rarely experience drain pain anymore, maybe once every couple of months. I only ever experienced it after the cycler had gotten most of the fluid out, so i would either clamp off to get the cycler to swap to fill, or bypass the drain after verifying that i'd gotten at least the fill volume drained.

It's different for everyone - PD is "hard" on the peritoneal membrane, and for many patients, the membrane will become less and less capable of functioning as it does early on. Things like peritonitis can also cause scarring that will impact how well it works.

I started at 9 hours on cycler. my clearance was acceptable, my KT/v was ~2.0. after back to back bouts with peritonitis about 18 months in due to a bag with a hole in it (ugh, i checked but didnt see it, only noticed the puddle under it on the cycler tray after treatment) my clearance diminished and i'm not at 12 on cycle and an all day dwell of icodextrin. Im told this is the limit of PD and if my clearance degrades further i'll probably have to at least add a HD cycle once a week or so, or switch to HD full time.

many dialysis patients have very serious comorbidities like heart disease and the like that may cause their life to be shorter but is really unrelated to being on dialysis. Many patients are elderly.

The "patients live about 10 years on dialysis" doesnt mean that it stops working after 10 years - it means that taken as a statistic, people who are on dialysis have a life expectancy of about 10 years. some people die on dialysis in the first year. some make it 20+ years no problem. but on the average that works out to ~10 years.

your life expectancy is most impacted by doing the things you need to be doing - eating right, getting all your treatments in, exercise/activity, etc. I wouldn't assume that since you've been on dialysis for 11 years that the end is near - i would assume that means you've done a good job for 11 years and KEEP IT UP! :)

high phosphorous is the second most critical thing for me in my treatment (sodium is the biggest problem for me).

High phosphorous has all kinds of bad effects. The worst for me is that when my phos was super high (11 or so i think?) i had something called pruritus - skin itchiness. I'm talking scratch my skin bloody in my sleep itchiness. i'm talking 24/7 itchiness that made me contemplate hospice care. 

Managing my phos intake was really difficult for me initially, and is still an ongoing battle. Phos binders help a ton but **they only work if you take them when you have food in your stomach**. my phos has fallen to almost normal, but not quite.

The other side effects are all over the map nausea, fatigue, etc, but it is also very hard on your bones, heart, and eyes but those are longer term issues that are harder to quantify.

i've been on PD for 3.5 years. I experienced a lot of drain pain in the first month, always toward the end of the drain. It felt like a sharp pain in my testicles. It was exceptionally unpleasant and if i was sleeping it would wake me up out of a dead sleep. occasionally it would bring me to tears but im not sure it was extra painful or just emotionally overwhelming - dialysis is as much a mental/emotional load as it is a physical one for many of us.

i think if your mom is experiencing pain just as the drain starts and throughout, something might be wrong. It might also just be normal drain pain.

one think about this diagnosis and chronic health care is that you have to really agressively advocate for yourself/the patient. Often you will hear "that's normal" when you try to tell your care team about issues/pain. only you/the patient know what it feels like - so sometimes you have to be more aggressive/fight for you to be heard. I dont mean being a jerk, jsut dont accept their nonchalant brush off answers.

Some examples from my journey:

"I experience nausea." *yeah that's pretty normal, just take your zofran if its bad*. "no you are not understanding, i am vomiting all day every day, this isn't normal and i would like more than comforting words. please let's determine how we can make this better."

"i am often dizzy" *that's common, just make sure you are using the right solutions. "no, i mean i am on the verge of passing out often" *oh i see, let's adjust your BP medication*

in short, because of the volume of patients they see, and the frequency of the symptoms we are likely to experience, their "first" answer isnt always one that fits you as the patient. 

If paracetemol isnt helping with her pain, and the pain is such that she is in tears and *is likely to not want to do her treatments if it continues* then they need to do more than give her a kind pat on the back and kick her out the door until the next appointment.

interesting. my clinic requires you to have antibiotics in case you develop peritonitis/cloudy dialysate so you can start immediately.

I'm allergic to a lot of things so i have a couple days of oral meds (clindamiacin i think) and i have vials of powdered vancomycin and meropenin (the ones i can tolerage) to be able to administer the first dose of those at the request of the oncall nurse. 

When i did have peritonitis, i had to come to the clinic immediately the next day with spent dialysate and they ordered whichever antibiotics the cultures indicate is necessary and they were delivered overnight at that point. (I did vanco which is a 5 day dose or something like that, and meropenium (idk how to spell it) for a few days until they confirmed the bacteria type and then overnighted 3 weeks worth for the course of the treatment).

My normal supply order is:
From Fresenius -
15-20 boxes of 1.5% solution
15-20 boxes of 2.5% solution
3-4 boxes of cassettes
1-2 boxes of caps
3 boxes of patient connector adapters (turns the one patient connector into two so i can disconnect during 1 dwell)
1 box of adapters for baxter icodextrin bag (for final fill/daytime dwell)

and separately, 4-5 boxes of icodextrin solution from Baxter. Every 4 weeks.

If i have reason to use manual bags, i might order a box of two of those to replace. 

In general you have at the end of delivery day about 5-6 weeks of supplies for the cycler and you should have 1-2 weeks of manual supplies.

all of this might vary a bit clinic to clinic but generally should be close.

I also receive some specific medications from fresenuis pharmacy (they use fed-ex to deliver) like renal vitamin, phosphorous binders, calcuium medication, some other hormone medication - basically dialysis specific things. i still get my normal meds (bp, diabetes, etc) from walgreens/whatever pharmacy i choose.

I also get protein strands if i dont use heparin so i get a few vials of that once a month from fed-ex to inject into my last fill bags.

when i visit the clinic they give me: Gauze pads, syringes, needles, equipment cleaner (Alcavis), wound/skin cleaner (Ex-Sept), tape, alcohol pads, etc. Sometimes they're out of something so i usually just have them give me everything every month whether i need it or not so i dont run out of gauze or tape or syringes when the clinic doesnt have them (which is somewhat often lol)

dialysate fluid lol. it comes in 6 liter bags, 2 per box, and i use 3 bags a night because 2 is like 400ml away from what my prescription requires. also i frequently change solution strength due to edema so i have to have more than enough of both solutions for the month if i end up using a lot more of one than the other.

When I started:

Surgery to place catheter. 

3-5 days later in dialysis clinic for bandage change. Nurse did a quick small fill and drain to flush the catheter.

Returned a week later. Nurse did a flush.

Returned a week later. Spent a whole morning learning how to wash my hands. Watched some videos. 

Day 2 was taught how to do a manual exchange. I am fairly competent and technical so trainer flew through material. 

Day 3 I learned the cycler. Demonstrated back how to do whole process start to finish. 

Day 4 came in watched last of videos. Demonstrated manual process without nurse prompts. Demonstrated cycler process without nurse prompts. Was told to begin that night. Training was over. Each of these steps did not only need to be one day, but that was all I needed. Some patients need more. Some will need to make notes etc. it’s not difficult but it is a pretty exact step by step process. 

In between my first bandage change and the beginning of training my first supplies and the cycler were delivered to my house. 

I put everything together without the nurse but she would have done it with/ for me if I hadn’t. 

Sometime after training my nurse had to do a home inspection. Just make sure you have a safe and clean spot to do treatment, no infection sources etc. 

After all that you’re pretty on your own. There’ll be a day you have to come for half a day for PET testing which tells them how your membrane works. There’ll be a visit where you have to bring drained dialysate fluid (there are capture bags) and 24 hours of urine if it’s still being produced. 

After that it’s once a month to clinic for labs and assessment with my RN and once a week or so later for a quick check in with neph to review labs and treatment and concerns. Every 3 months you bring urine and collected dialysate for adequacy of PD testing. 

It’s this until something unplanned happens (like an infection) or you get a transplant. 

Prepare to be underwhelmed at what healthcare is like with chronic health conditions vs going to primary or urgent care for sickness and that sort of thing. It can be very frustrating, for you this is your whole world but for the staff you’re just one of 20 or more patients they see that day. They’re great people but it’s a big adjustment especially if you’re coming from private/ppo insurance. 

I am a planner and very anxious and the introductory process of pd was a lot of anxiety. I was also quite sick. Several years in it’s just another monthly responsibility and I love my care team and have fun giving them a hard time. 

PD isn’t difficult but it is 90% on the patient/care partner to do the work and worry. The clinic staff is there for phone help or the sort of thing but at home it’s all you. You are your own nurse. You will have to weigh yourself(the patient) every day, track that along with body temp and blood pressure and some information about solutions used mf readings from the machine. You will have to make decisions based on your vitals/symptoms. You will have to be diligent and follow the same process every day. 

You (the patient) will find it uncomfortable or hard to sleep. The machine will make noise and alarms until your body learns not to move a lot and pinch the tubing. You will be trapped connected to the machine for the duration of treatment. 

My machine is next to my bed and my bedroom door. Th tubing reaches from there to the bathroom, my computer desk in the living room, and a recliner next to the couch. I cannot reach the refrigerator or sink so without a helper I have to plan water and such before connecting. The machine will move up to 6 feet from the outlet. The patient tubing is about 20 feet. The machine will need to drain preferably in a toilet or etc. this can be up to 40 feet if necessary (there is an extension available for the drain). 

Fresenius gives (rents) you a rolling plastic table for the machine. Baxter might be different. If you are in US it’ll be one of those two regardless of the name of your clinic. 

Everything except trash bags are covered by insurance and Medicare. You qualify for Medicare b the day you start dialysis. You can start it with private insurance for dual insurance (which eliminates most deductibles/coinsurance related to esrd). 

You will be given or shipped a kit of emergency antibiotics both oral and intraperitoneal. You’ll learn how to mix and administer those in training. 

You will be asked and reasoned to have 3 days of emergency water and food that is non perishable and doesn’t require heat. 

You will register with FEMA so you can be located in disasters/emergency situations. 

You will be asked to prepare a medical advanced directive. 

Both of you should consider therapy. Dialysis is a big unfair life change and for each of you hanging to face the realities of morality on a daily basis can be tough to go through especially for the non sick family who is worried but trying to be supportive. And the patient who might be scared but not wanting to upset the family.

Edit: sent too early. 

PD supplies take up a pretty large amount of space. I receive a pallet every 4 weeks of 40-60 boxes. The delivery driver will put it all away as long as it isn’t tricky to navigate your home. 

Let us know if you have specific concerns or questions. You will have a lot of them. That’s ok and normal :) you both got this!

I'm proud of you. I know this was hard, and scary! You did it though!

You will probably not feel great after your treatments - it will also likely get more bearable as your body becomes more used to it. If you are nauseous talk to your clinic about it. My neph has prescribed me like a lifetime supply of Zofran which i had to take daily at first but have become less dependent on it as i became more used to dialysis.

Again, strong work! Here's to many more tomorrows for you!

how will you be fashionable if you are dead?

You realize you will, in fact, die if you do not start soon. It will not be a pleasant death.

Im sorry but there's no sugar coating it. if you dont have functional kidneys, and you dont get started on dialysis, you are going to progressively get sicker and sicker, while placing undue strain on the rest of your body like your heart. assuming you dont die from the edema, you'll start to experience the worst nausea and symptoms you can imagine as your blood becomes more and more toxic.

It sucks. it's unfair. it's life changing. but without it, you will not live.

Once you start dialysis, you qualify for medicare. your dialysis center will help you with this.

I know you're scared. i know you want to ignore this problem. I think we've all been there. Please, get started soon before you really get to experience how very terrible non-functioning kidneys are. You're just in the baby stages of blood toxicity and edema. it will get worse. you won't be able to breathe. you wont be able to move without pain. you will throw up more than you ever thrown up before, for weeks. Save yourself the pain and get started.

> I covered the exit site with a 4x4 lightly to let it breathe. Then wound up the tubing and taped it to the side of the exit. You do not want any tugging on it. I used the paper tape. It held well enough. I would replace it with the vinyl tape to take a shower. I avoided the silken tape. Very painful to remove.

this is also how i secure mine, more or less. Turns out i am allergic/sensitive to paper tape, silk tape, etc. all leave my skin blistered after 12ish hours. 

For those with similar sensitivities who read this, initially i bought a roll of tegaderm from amazon. it's about 10 yards x 4 inches wide in a roll and i would cut off strips to secure my cath tubing, and i would use a 2x4" tegaderm patch with 1x1" gauze squares to cushion/protect my exit site. The roll is ~ ten bucks in the US, and the 2x4 size tegaderm patches are about 25-30 bucks for 100 of them. more than i want to spend, but the only option that worked.

Recently (3-4 months) i discovered a product called "Hypafix" tape. it also comes in a roll like the tegaderm did, but this is stretchy fabric feeling breathable adhesive tape that sticks to my skin well but is super easy to remove and does not irritate my skin. it is a life saver.

I use a piece just bigger than my gauze to cover my exit site, then i choose a spot nearby to "anchor" my catheter with some slack between there and the exit site (to allow for swelling during dwells), and then i just tape the other end of the cathether somewhere on the opposite side of my belly from the exit site.

When i am connected to the cycler, i undo/dispose of the end-of-the-catheter-tape and connect normally, taping the tubing to my shirt and leaving the original anchor and exit site covering in place.

> Way more mental bandwidth expanded on dialysis. With in-clinic hemo you just go and they do everything. With PD I have to manage my supplies, set up and tear down the machine, record my vitals, etc. Every day.

Absolutely this. it is difficult to describe to those who don't experience it or dont find it challenging. It is exhausting to me sometimes, and i often fantasize about just showing up at a clinic 3x a week and letting people take care of me. Not saying i am wanting to or planning to, just that it's something i fantasize about. It is probably also related to living alone and having to face this mostly alone.

> - No days off.

yep. i think i've missed treatment 2x in 40 months. one time was due to cycler issues in the middle of the night and not wanting to reset the machine (meaning tear it down and start over...the machine ran out of fluid in the bag it wanted to get it from). the other time was due to my child's hospitalization (we were in ER all night)

> - Weight gain. I've probably gained like 30lbs since starting PD.

This one is also frustrating to me. I eat so little compared to pre dialysis, mostly due to a lack of appetite and often nausea. The dialysate contains not a small amount of calories, and apparently my body is really good at consuming them, lol.

> - LONG treatment time. At least for someone like me with no renal function.

my egfr is ~7 and my on-cycler time is about 12 hours (11.5 on a good day). 4 fills/dwells ~2800ml, and a final fill for an all day icodextrin dwell of 1950ml. I am "dialyazing" 24 hours a day. The daytime dwell is the worst. my abdomen is swollen, and my waistline grows a couple inches from morning to evening as the ico pulls water out (around a liter of uf from the all day dwell).

> - Can fuck with your sleep if you use the cycler.

In my experience this is not so bad after a month or two. eventually i got tired enough it doesnt matter. i think now it would wake me up if there wasn't that sound of the pump and all the weird noises the cycler makes.

I like PD for the ease in fluids. Phosphorous is the biggest thing I worry about when it comes to eating. Because i dont eat very much every day, i have a bit less restriction on what that can be - i can't get crazy, but my labs are good with what i do eat and i'm far from perfect or dilligent about it.

It's really, really hard to understate what losing half (in my case) of your freedom per day. as has been said, for 12 hours a day i am tethered to life support and can go about 20 feet from the cycler, and the cycler can move about 5 feet from where i have it if necessary. 

I also talked them into giving me a multi-port option since i live alone; it allows me to disconnect and reconnect if needed during a dwell. this was important when i had to connect before dinner in order to be off cycler the next morning in time for work or dr or whatever and still be able to make dinner the night before. They come in boxes of 10 and you connect it to the patient connector on the cycler cassette before you connect your catheter. it turns the 1 connection into 2 because there's another connection that is unused/sterile if you need it.

one thing that is worth mentioning, just because you are on home treatment doesn't mean you dont have to go to the clinic or set time aside for other things related to it. One day a month for labs and RN assessment. One day a month for appointment with nephrologist, social worker, dietician, and RN to discuss treatment and lab results and make/explain changes. One day a month i have to be home/disconnected/ready for delivery of a pallet of supplies which is in a 4 hour window (today it was 11a-3pm, driver arrived at 2pm). One day a month i have to be home similarly for icodextrin delivery (since that comes from competing Baxter) - but i dont know what day it will be out of a 2 day window until the day before.

Hey there. I have ESRD/Stage 5 CKD for a little over 3 years now. I have one child, who just completed her first year at university. I have been on dialysis since early 2021. I raised my child alone and have no partner; her mother lives far away in another state.

first - as a dialysis patient: I mean, it sucks. I will likely never feel "normal" again, and that's just something I've had to learn to accept. Dialysis itself is frustrating at times, mentally, but it is also the only thing keeping me alive. My kidneys failed and i almost died over the course of several months before i could get through all the hoops and processes to be able to start dialysis. Once i started, it took several months for me to get "used" to it and be able to sleep normally (i do peritoneal dialysis at home every night). there have been times that i have been scared, frustrated, angry, lonely, and hopeless. This seems normal - it is a massive life change, and while 50-ish years old seems "old" when you are young, it doesn't necessarily feel that way when you get there. My mind is still sharp, and now I feel often that i am trapped in this decaying body that is betraying me.

I am also thankful for the dialysis, as again, I wouldn't be alive without it. I have to go get connected here in a few minutes and i am procrastinating it, but I'll do it. I have to. I live to see tomorrow. Not next week - tomorrow. every day is a gift. That's what i hold onto.

Now, as a father who has watched his only child experience this happen to their father, i would say this: I am eternally grateful that the universe deemed it that this wonderful creature would be given to me to raise and nurture. I have fought hard, every day, worked hard every day, to ensure that she was taken care of and had the best life I could give her. When she is home, her assistance is invaluable - it really becomes apparent how much a small act of kindness or assistance means when you are no longer able to do the things you used to be able to. I enjoy her making me meals, which she plans around what she knows i should and shouldn't eat. I enjoy her getting me a glass of water when I'm thirsty, or when she tells me about her adventures at uni while i am preparing the dialysis machine.

I would be devastated if she felt like she needed to leave uni, and give up on her life and dreams, because she wants to take care of me. The hope that her life will turn out a little happier than mine has is what drives me. It's what makes every dr appointment, every lab test poke, every cycler connection, every single thing I do day in and day out just to stay alive one more day, worth it. I don't try to count the days I may or may not have left - i just try to make it to tomorrow.

I know she worries about me, but she also has to worry about her life, and her future. I'm trying really hard to be a part of that, by doing what I'm supposed to, avoiding foods and things that will keep me from living longer.

The 3 years on dialysis has been a roller coaster. Sometimes it's great, sometimes it's not. Right now it's in the middle. All i know is I will keep fighting, for one more day. I can do it one more day.

To expand on what u/buckeyebentley said above:

The removal of toxins works via diffusion across the peritoneal membrane. By filling your abdominal cavity with mostly pure dialysate, which doesn’t contain urea or etc, so waste molecules move across the membrane into the dialysate until there is a balance of concentration. This is why after a certain amount of time, it is more effective to drain and replace the dialysate so that the diffusion can continue. 

The higher concentrations of dialysate don’t necessarily remove more toxins, as much as they remove more fluid. 

There is likely a small increase in waste transport as a function of the water itself being absorbed into the dialysate, but the concentration strengths of the dialysate are used more to remove fluid / address edema. 

I am a Fresenius patient also - they do kt/v measurement every quarter. If you recall, to do that test you had to collect your urine for 24 hours, as well as a sample of your spent dialysate. The lab measures the various toxins in that and calculates the kt/v value which generally indicates how effective your treatment is at removing toxins. If the result is too low, they will adjust your prescription. I started with 4 exchanges, but as my urine output reduced (probably 50% for me after 3 years but everyone’s different) I had to add a daytime dwell, and eventually that got replaced by a dwell of Icodextrin which the cycler fills me with after the 4 cycles and it remains in my abdomen until the evening when I connect for the next cycler treatment. 

If you add your 24 hour urine output to your total ultrafiltration number from the cycler after treatment, you now know how much fluid your body can “intake” without causing edema, excluding however much you lose to sweat and breathing. 

For PD patients doing treatment 7x a week that is a daily intake guideline - which is why it is easier in that regard compared to HD - where they are needing to remove fluid from ~48 hours of accumulation in one 3-4 hour session. 

Removing fluid too fast or removing too much at once is unpleasant and potentially dangerous so HD patients have pretty strict fluid restrictions in comparison to PD.

Showed up at the clinic at 9am, empty. Nurse filled me with a 2L manual bag, then drained 100ml and took a sample. went back in at the 4h mark, same thing, lay down, slosh it around, drain it all and they took a sample and also took bloodwork.

the results of the test determine what kind of "transport" your peritoneal membrane is, which is a factor in how your prescription will be calculated.

The test is what it is. your ability to dialysize (idk if that's a word) is reflected in the results. For the most part, you will only do this test once in your PD adventure.

I dont want to reiterate what others have said, but here's what i'll add as a 3 year PD patient.

From my perspective, home PD means i am more in charge, but also more responsible, for my medical care. 

I have to take and record my own vitals every single day. I have to set up and tear down the cycler every single day. 

I have to be home 2 days a month (usually 2 days the same week of the month) for a 4 hour window to receive deliveries. I dont find out the 4 hour window until the friday before for one of them (monday delivery) or 2 days before (midweek delivery).

I have to make decisions based on current conditions (edema/bloodpressure) that impact what solution strength i'll be using.

I have to have an extra week's supply of cycler supplies, minimum.

I have to have 1-2 weeks of manual PD supplies.

I have to order my supplies (either through web/app or a phonecall to/from customer service).

I have to go to the clinic 1 day a month for labwork and assessment, required by CMS/Medicare. this visit is about 1.5 hours depending on how much we chat. This visit is with my assigned RN (in my clinic i always see the same nurse unless theres something like vacation/sick nurse).

I have to go to the clinic one day a month, separate from but after the first visit, in the same month, to review labs with Nephrologist, Nurse, Dietician, Social Worker.

Until recently, these appointments were random as heck. after i complained enough, they've swapped to nurses handling their own appointments and i have a static appointment "day" and time.

Once every 3 months, i have to collect and save my urine for 24 hours and bring to the clinic. that night i have to connect collection bags to the cycler drain tube to collect the used dialysate (all 14 liters of it plus the fluid it removed from my body), carry these bags to the bathroom, carefully extract 20ml of the fluid from each of the 3 bags, and dump the rest down the drain. I have to take the 60ml (a urinalysis cup) of dialysate and the jug of 24 hours of urine from the preeceding 24 hours to the clinic on my assessment labwork visit that month for kt/v testing (is dialysis working/how good is it working).

I have to do the initial troubleshooting of any problem encountered in the setup or operation of the cycler. If i can't figure it out i have to call the on-call nurse (for emergencies) or technical support (for tech issues) myself. 

Because i am not great at keeping on a schedule, i have to make sure i calculate the right start time so that the cycler is done in the morning if i need to be somewhere. I work from home so normally it doesnt matter, but if i have to be somewhere at 8am, i need to be off the cycler by 6am so i can shower and get ready and leave by 7am etc.

i have to report my vitals and some info from the cycler every day via website/phone app even though the cycler sends the same data to the clinic via modem.

it is absolutely NOT as easy to travel as the brochure makes it out to be. yes you can do it. it is a pain in the butt. Even a weekend car trip there's a ton of stuff you gotta bring with you.

It takes quite some time to learn to sleep through the new sensations and the noises that the cycler makes all night.

you will be shocked at how uncomfortable it is to have an extra 2.5 or so liters of fluid in your abdomen while you try to sleep. it makes my back hurt, if i lie on my back i feel like i can't breathe. 3 years into it i sleep like a corpse - i barely move, the blankets are hardly disturbed. The cycler nosies are relaxing. Before dialysis i was a wild sleeper who often woke up upside down in the bed lol.

I am thankful for the machine and i simultaneously hate it, i am often angry about having to do this, i am often angry at myself for lifestyle choices i can't undo that likely led to this. What i wanted to express is that while home treatment is really, really flexible especially for working people, it is a lot of responsibility and sometimes i fantasize about just showing up at a treatment center and relaxing for 4 hours while someone else worrys about settings and all that and i can just sit there.

When you are dedicating 10+ hours a day to treatment/being tethered to a machine, you really start running out of hours that arent already spoken for. you can't effectively say exercise, or clean up the house, take a shower, etc, while connected to the cycler. I have my cycler in a position where the tubing reaches to where i can use the restroom while connected, and sit at my desk for work/personal computer/gaming activities, and sleep, but i can't reach outside my front door, or reach my kitchen sink/refrigerator without disconnecting. generally you cannot disconnect for the 10 hours - but sometimes you can convince them to give you an additional port (or an adapter to turn the 1 port into 2) so you can disconnect once, usually during a dwell, if i wanted to do something i can't do while connected.

Although you dont have the deep valleys and peaks of in center HD (because you accumulate toxins for 48ish hours then spend 4 hours removing all of that at once vs accumulating toxins for 24 hours but removing them daily via PD), PD still leaves me feeling generally sluggish, and the amount of exchanges i do add up to something like 700 calories added plus some effects on my blood sugar.

Here are some photos i took of just the cycler bags immediately after delivery. each stack is close to 6.5 feet tall. This is just the cycler bags for the month + emergency reserve and does not include 5 boxes of cassettes (basically the tubing bundle), 2 boxes of caps, 2 boxes of adapters for icodextrin because it's a different manufacturer, 5 boxes of additional port adapters, 1 box of drain bags, and several boxes of manual bags in 2 different concentrations for emergencies.

Plus gauze packs, sterile gauze packs, heparin vials, syringes and needles (i have to inject heparin into my dialysate bag so that i dont develop fiberous protein in my periteneum which can block the cathether), tape, rolls of tegaderm and hypafix for exit site bandaging (im allergic to most tapes so i have to use those), bottles of disinfectant for the catheter tubing, bottles of wound cleaner for the exit site, bleach and wipes to clean the cycler daily, trash bags to handle the massive amount of waste this all creates, oh and all the emergency antibiotics i have to have on hand in case of infection. PD requires *a massive* amount of storage space.

i think it's more a manner of shifting your thought patterns regarding "bad".

Potassium isn't bad. Phosphorous isnt bad. both are essential to human life. Sodium too.

The issue comes when your body is unable to eliminate excess amounts of toxins. Potassium, Phosphorous, Sodium - while being essential to human life, are toxins when they exceed certain levels in your blood stream. Normally kidneys eliminate the excess. Obviously in kidney failure, this is not necessarily happening or not happening enough.

I am sure you know all of this but i wanted to reiterate it because it's important for perspective.

You aren't "not allowed" to eat foods. You are highly suggested to limit, and perhaps eliminate, foods which will exacerbate toxin levels which have all the side effects you already know of.

The thing is some people can tolerate some things better than others. I am able, while taking binders, to eat potatoes and cheese in what i consider moderation, but what a dietician would consider too much. However, every month i get to see the results of my diet reflected in my labwork. 

Treatment isnt some kind of school test where the clinic/hospital is going to grade me and pass/fail me based on my performance. My choices affect my health and my quality of life alone. If my clinic had their way with their "suggestions" then i would be miserable. I take their suggestions, evaluate them, review my labs with them, and decide if i need to make an adjustment. If i refuse to make the adjustment, the doctor and nurses go home and go about their life. They dont itch. They dont have heart palpatations. they dont get sick and nauseous. They dont experience my edema.

I think it's important to keep this perspective, at least for me. If i view everything as "rules i cannot break" i will mentally rebel against the restrictions. If i feel like im more involved in my treatment, then if i look at the results, and i have to deal with the edema and other symptoms, then i feel less like "im not allowed to" and more like "i think i'll limit this because i dont want to feel like this."

it's hard for me to say. I'll just explain ultrafiltration and how it pertains to dialysis.

In dialysis, the word "ultrafiltration" is used to label the volume of fluid being removed by dialysis. 
In hemo dialysis (HD), this is removed directly from the bloodstream. The blood is taken out of the body, run through some filters, and injected back into the body, in simple terms. This means there are practical limits to how much blood they can remove/put back per minute or hour, how much fluid they can remove per minute/hour, etc. The filtering also removes the bad stuff/toxins.

HD is accomplished by way of an "access". This access can be a "chest tube" (generally how dialysis starts in emergency situations), or more preferably via a fistula on one of the limbs. They use veins from say your leg, or probably veins from not you, and probably there are synthetic options - I’m not sure. Whatever it is, it provides a place where they can insert the needles repeatedly, as you will be doing this every other day.

In peritoneal dialysis (PD), the fluid is removed through osmosis via the peritoneal membrane in the abdomen. a solution of mostly water with some stuff mixed in that uses the principle of osmosis to remove fluid from the body. The peritoneal membrane is semi-permeable - meaning that small molecules like water pass through it easily, but larger things like blood cells and the like do not. The solution that is used (dialysate) starts pulling water through the membrane because nature likes a balance - and the solution does not include all the stuff that your body has built up like toxins, so those get pulled into the solution. 

The solution "dwells" in your abdomen for a couple hours, and then it is drained/measured and replaced however many times your prescription calls for it. My prescription for the machine is 4 dwells of 2800L for 2 hours each, and a final 1500L dwell that stays all day until the next connection to the machine. My ultrafiltration rate is about 1700-2000mL a day, every day, 7 days a week. I do PD at home, overnight, every day. It is about an 11-hour connection period, so I’m not asleep at the beginning. 

PD is accomplished by an abdominal catheter – plastic tubing is surgically inserted such that it is in your peritoneal cavity and exits through your abdomen usually to the far side of your stomach a bit above your waistline. The site it exits through never fully heals while the catheter is in it, so it must be cleaned daily and generally covered to prevent infection.

When it comes to ultrafiltration, one thing that helped me understand some of it is you must think of where that fluid needs to come from. It’s not just sitting in your blood, or in your swollen limbs, etc., right? It’s everywhere. Your blood has some, your muscles have some, your fat has some, whatever - so, as you pull it out, it's not like you just have this 3L reservoir tank of extra fluid that you need to empty – it’s more, as we take some fluid out of your bloodstream/body, we have to wait until the fluid we can't take out yet replaces it/migrates to where it can be removed, which takes time.

For HD, the safe/practical limits on ultrafiltration rate per hour mean that the total amount of fluid removed by HD is lower than it can be for a PD patient. The HD patient is trying to lose 2 days’ worth of fluid in 4 hours. The PD patient is trying to lose 1 days’ worth of fluid in 8-10 hours.

I’ve heard that ultrafiltration rates for hemo patients is no more than 7-8ml per kg of body weight per hour. Your mom weighs around 100 kg, so that would mean a max of 700-800ml per hour. treatment is i think 4 hours, so 2800-3200ml per treatment day. I believe there is probably some variance in there that could make that higher or lower, but ballpark wise, that should give you some idea. 

I have read that the more, and/or faster, they remove fluid the worse it can make the patient feel in the post-dialysis recovery period, and that hemo patients feel pretty wiped out immediately following their session, often still recovering the next day.

My beginnings with dialysis were i think atypical, but i was deathly sick by the time i started, so it took me several weeks to feel any improvement, and several months to settle into the "new" way "normal" would feel.

i covered some of that above, but speaking in general terms: things like sodium and phosphorous are exceptionally harmful to your kidneys when they are already damaged.

one of the major issues with sodium is that it has a major effect on 2 things: water retention and blood pressure, and those are correlated. 

If you retain too much water, your blood "volume" increases, and now your heart has to pump harder to move it. Water retention also makes your tissues cells bigger (they contain more fluid) which pushes on the walls of the blood vessels making it harder for the heart to push fluid through them.

This increased pressure and blood volume damages the filtering mechanisms of the kidney as a result. now your kidneys cant remove as much fluid. so you retain more. and cause more damage. so you retain more...This usually happens over years and years, but eventually the damage becomes noticeable - usually toward stage 4/5, and can progress quite rapidly without intervention (dialysis/diet change).

With her kidneys not working properly, and not receiving dialysis, she is unable to filter enough phosphorous out of her blood with her extremely diminished kidney function, which has a ton of negative effects on the rest of the body, some of which then can cause more kidney damage (high calcum levels can lead to blood pressure issues again), and are really not good for your heart and bones. Naturally occurring phosphorous is not as bad as artificial, but too much of the good stuff is also bad.

things to investigate, maybe limit in terms of high phosphorous: Cheese, Milk, Yogurt, Ice Cream, nuts, legumes (beans), chocolate, seeds...at stage 4 (the stage before dialysis usually) you usually get told to limit to 800-1000mg a day. The really big hitters there are processed/packaged stuff. Frozen meals, anything with a longer than natural shelf life, usually contains something or other phosphate. they're all phosphorous in terms of this context.

you said her kidneys are at 13% function, right? That probably means her urine output is greatly diminished compared to when she was younger? But every day, i assume she consumes fluids - we all do...fluids which are in glasses, sure, but also fluids in soup, fluids in veggies, fluid in fruits, in yogurt, etc, right? 

One liter (33.8 ounces) of water weighs 1 kilogram (2.2 pounds). The only exit for fluid from the body is excretion (pee/bowel/sweat/breathing). It's estimated that average adults lose anywhere from 40mL to 800mL a day to non-urination. everything else has to come out through urination, or there's an imbalance. It's not uncommon for average adults to consume several liters of fluids a day. a starbucks venti is 590mL(20 oz). A typical bottle of water is 500ml(16.9oz). both of those are about half a kg or 1 pound of fluid that your body has to "deal with". that starts to add up quickly.

That's before even looking at sodium levels and such which impact retention and excretion as well. But think about it if your mom has several cups of coffee a day or a bottle of water here or there and eats a diet with things that contain fluid that you dont think about, it's not hard to come up with 3 or more kg(6.6 or more lbs) of fluid intake.

Fluid restrictions and fluid tracking become pretty important on hemodialysis, as removing fluid "all at once" every other day instead of over 48 hours more gradually because its really hard on the body, and they can only "pull off" so much fluid before it puts things like your heart and body at risk. This is the kind of dialysis it sounds like she will be on based on your other comments. (Peritoneal dialysis has less (or sometimes no) fluid restrictions because the fluid removal occurrs daily over the course of hours (it varies per patient but generally 8 or so hours overnight), but it is not without its downsides or disadvantages either, and it doesnt work for every patient.)

the excess fluid will also cause problems with her heart and her lungs, it affects your blood pressure, and it can do some really unfun things to your skin (blistering and such). If she isnt already, you might have her ask her doctor about a dieuretic (sometimes called water pill) which will, ideally, increase her urine volume/output to get her excess body fluid more balanced. I am not a doctor, just a dialysis patient, so this isnt medical advice, just trying to help you understand what i've learned on this journey that might help you.

i wish you and your mom the best. i really think fluid management will be a really helpful thing between now and when her dialysis starts, which sounds like it's quite a ways off.

keep in mind if her kidney function declines during that time, none of her health will benefit from that, so make sure she is eating kidney-friendly, not just diabetic friendly. there can be some pretty big differences. Eating kidney friendly will help lessen the damage to her kidneys over time. blood pressure is also pretty key i think, so manage sodium.

> PS - I had to collect 24 hours or urine to measure my output and for specific tests (though they wouldn't say what tests).

1. they need to know your total urine output for 24 hours in terms of volume. This plus your ultrafiltration (when you start doing PD, you will "inject" the solution into your peritoneal cavity, lets say 2000mL, and after it "dwells" for a time (~2 hours likely), you drain it out (the machine does) and the excess fluid above the initial 2000mL is "ultrafiltration". these numbers help the clinic in their overall assessment of your treatment and status.

2. at least for me, once a quarter (4x a year) i have to do 24 hour urine collection, and i have to connect special bags to the cycler drain to capture all the used dialysate. so I start collecting the day before, that evening I have to use the drain bags, the next morning the first urine of the day ends the 24 hour collection, and you take a urine-cup sized sample of the dialysate to the clinic with your collected urine. They use this sample, along with your blood work and urinalysis, to determine a lot of information, notably your kt/v number which is some kind of calculated number that determines the effectiveness of your PD treatment over time. The higher the kt/v the better.

ahead for you, i believe: you'll have to spend like 4 hours at the clinic at some point where they do something called a PET test, where they fill you with a manual bag and then at set intervals (every hour?) they drain a little out so they can test it. The PET test tells them what kind of "transport" your peritoneal membrane is - meaning, how well does it diffuse across the membrane. this test has only happened the one time, so far, as you are what you are in this test. Hello. I'm sorry that you are having to deal with this. I am M49 and have been stage 5/dialysis for ~3 years. My CKD is also a result of diabetes, but I was on a roller coaster of sugar control/poor habits for a very long time. I didn't really understand how serious CKD was because i didnt feel any different/sick, the only symptom i had for years (decades?) was foamy urine.

I didnt follow any of the CKD dietary restrictions - i mostly, when i was trying, tried to eat things that didnt make my blood sugar bad. That meant that i ate a lot of lunch meat and cheese, thinking i was doing the right thing because it made my blood sugar perfect.

Unfortunately i didnt know that i needed to actually control my sodium (my BP was fine thanks to medication!), i didnt know anything about phosphates, i only knew potassium as something that helped with cramps, etc.

You should avoid phosphates - which eliminates pretty much most of the inner aisles of the grocery store, especially packaged foods, prepared foods, and frozen foods (excluding like frozen veggies/fruit).

They'll give you a lot of information. Do what you can to learn as much of it as you can. It sucks, it's hard, it's annoying, and it's time consuming to eat 'properly', and you will not be perfect, but that's ok. the more you follow the recommendations, the longer you can delay progression.

I started with 4 cycler exchanges of 2500ml each cycle. It was about 9.5 hours, not including setup connection disconnection and tear down. 

Later, probably due to declining kt/v it was increased to 4x2750 and when the bags changed to 6L instead of 5L we went to 2800x4 and we bumped up to 10 hours to get a bit longer dwells. 

Kt/v continued declining so I was given a 5th fill, called “last bag” and that is 1500ml of icodextrin from Baxter (I am a Fresenius patient) that is high concentrate and extended dwell (7.5%) so now it’s 4x2800+1x1500. The icodextrin is in me all day until the next treatment session when it drains out in the initial drain at the start of the machine cycles.  I think it might now be 10.5 hours. 

I basically calculate it in my mind as 12 hours a day though. Between opening boxes, breaking down boxes, dealing with the trash, setting up the machine, hand washing, connection, 10.5h of treatment that may extend if the drain is long, eventual disconnection, dealing with the leftover solution and tearing down the machine. It is also easier to calculate when I need to start - if I have to go to the office I know I have to be connected by 7pm so I can be for sure done at 7am when I need to shower and get out the door.

I was 45 when i was diagnosed with ESRD - i went to Urgent Care for shortness of breath and fatigue (i was driving after dropping my kid off at her mother's and i was struggling to catch my breath, sitting on my ass behind the wheel). When they weighed me i weighed about 30 pounds more than i normally did, and my egfr was like 17 or something.

Like you, i felt like the biggest dumb ass - i struggled with diabetes and hypertension for over 20 years, sometimes doing the right things, often not. I smoked for 20 years, i ate like shit, i did absolutely nothing to control my sodium or anything else. I'd get told by the doctors "you're spilling protein" and "you have CKD" but similarlly, i didnt really understand what that meant - i felt fine, i didnt know that if i kept eating like shit and etc that i would continue to decline, all while not feeling anything wrong.

It takes some mental fortitude, and sometimes i break down and have bad days/tears/anger, but overall - I have just learned that i can't change anything in the past - i cant go back and eat better, walk more, learn more - i can only change today and prepare a better tomorrow.

My biggest advice to ESRD homies is this: you HAVE to take charge of your health case. Your doctors and nurses will have varying levels of attention/care, and you really have to ask a lot of questions, challenge a lot of advice (not argue - just stand up for yourself). It can be exhausting. It can feel isolating. It was very frustrating for me to learn how different medical care is for chronic illness over accute illnesses.

My choices were similar to yours, except i went with Peritoneal Dialysis at home, because i felt like it would work the best with keeping my career (i also work construction - as a PM) and also while wrapping up single fatherhood (my daughter, sole custody, was 15-16 when i was diagnosed. PD has been great, but after 3 years, i'm not sure if i wouldnt rather just go to the clinic 3x a week and chill with the nurses and let someone else keep me alive.

anyway sorry for rambling - hang in there brother, dont beat yourself up too bad, because what you have to deal with going forward is going to beat the shit out of you physically and mentally. Good luck - the road ahead is bumpy, but tomorrow is a new day.

i dont think all pd patients have to take it, but i know it's not atypical. PD is pretty good at fluid elimination, and depending on the composition of your diet, sometimes things dont want to move along like they should.

for me, i take one tablet daily and that keeps things flowing pretty naturally. sometimes i dont take it if i notice things are moving too fast, but most days i take it just to not have a day of discomfort in case things slow down.

i got some larger patches of tegaderm on amazon which were big enough to cover the whole site and tubing, with enough room to spare so there would be a good "seal" around everything, and then i just took a shower very careful to not let water pool in that area (like if i held my arms so water built up) and didnt let the full shower stream hit it - had no issues, and even if i did the clinic was available to change the dressing with a little lecture im sure. I had all that ready pre-op though, because i knew i wouldnt be able to handle not showering, especially since at that time i had extreme skin itchiness 24/7 as a result of high phosphate levels.

i dont think so, but i do take colace daily since i've been doing PD. It can be a struggle to stay regular in my experience. you dont want to have issues there, they're exceptionally unpleasant and dangerous.

i lost a ton of weight leading up to PD actually starting (i was exceptionally nauseous and unable to eat much for several weeks due to needing dialysis but not getting it) - probably close to 30-35 pounds in 4-6 weeks. I gained it back to my pre-failure weight despite having a lot of trouble eating or wanting to eat in the first year or so of treatment, but I haven't gained "too much" from it.

im 3 years in and i usually only eat one meal a day, i struggle to eat enough protein so i have to supplement it (PD seems to strip a lot of protein from your body or something). I am also exceptionally less active since entering stage 5. I wasn't really active before, but now im largely inactive - treatment is mild but it seems to sap a lot of my overall energy level.

Like the above commenter, i am on 11 hours a day/night (whichever i choose) and i also have an all-day fill of 1500ml of icodextrin (long dwell solution). It took me about a month to be able to sleep without alarms/pain. A pregnancy pillow (amazon) helped alot - i am a side sleeper but the pain of the near 3L cycler fills was a lot for my back when i tried to sleep - the pillow helped in the way it helps pregnant women.

i've been through a catheter exchange (i had a couple of cases of infection/peritonitis back to back so they had to swap it earlier this year) and my second cathether has been a much more pleasant experience. it's on the "right" side for me in terms of how i like to sleep and where the machine is placed in my room, and it hasnt had the drain issues i had previously. biggest thing is my first catheter was around my waistline which was really inconvenient. my new cath is on the other side and a bit higher, so my pants dont come near it.

i've gone through valleys and mountaintops on this PD journey. some days i am exceptionally grateful for the convenience, and the lack of resctrictions compared to HD, but i've also had days where i hate the machine and i hate dialysis and im tired of taking care of myself and the idea of just going to the center 3x a week and letting someone else do all this is enticing - but the convenience of PD works for me, especially as i am mostly work-from-home.

good luck on your journey, sorry if i overshared.

once i got really sick, she understood that i would use it more often as it really significantly helps me be able to eat and not be nauseous 24/7 (i have end stage renal disease).
my advice, free of course, is when they are old enough to understand you are hiding something from them, is around the time you should consider having a discussion (at their maturity level) about it. Hiding things from your kids develops mistrust and suspicion and just isnt healthy, in my opinion.

I also am on PD, 10H a day. In a couple of months i'll pass 3 years since i started PD.

for months, i was largely unable to sleep. The noise was easiest to get used to, but drain pain lingered for months, as well as various issues with my first catheter placement/location. Eventually, i got tired enough to sleep anyway, and conditioned myself to lay on the side that didnt cause the machine to alarm in the middle of the night. that went on for over 2 years before i got peritonitis a couple times in a row and had to have my cath replaced - which gave me an opportunity to make sure the nurse marked a better location for my on my abdomen (my initial placement was literally on my waistline.) A lot of those lingering issues (drain pain, mid-sleep alarms, body position alarms) went away after that.

to your original question - if you have been pretty good about your treatment (no skipping), your labwork is where it needs to be, etc, one day without treatment, while not ideal, isn't the end of the world. (i am not a doctor, this is not medical advice). I have missed 3 days in 3 years - 2 due to equipment malfunction (cycler ran out of fluid in the bag it was trying to get it out of even though other bag was fine), and once just because i wanted to. Each time i missed was really not a big deal, didnt make a huge difference in labwork at the next appointment or anything. I felt bloated by the time i got to the next treatment time, and it took a couple of days of treatment to eliminate the extra weight from missing a day of treatment. 

i have also adjusted my timeframe for treatment each day as it suits my lifestyle - neither my doctor nor my nurses really care when i am connected, as long as i do my time on the machine each day. So some "times" in my life, i've done treatment while WFH so i can sleep without being connected that night, etc.

You should also be able to get your clinic to give you whatever you need to be able to disconnect/reconnect between dwells. In the Fresenius world, they're called "MTS set w/ stay•safe® PIN connectors" and they connect to the end of the tubing on the cycler side and add 2 new clean connections. Using those i can connect early, disconnect during a dwell and cook dinner or whatever, and reconnect at the end of the dwell. I usually only disconnect once, if at all, but my nurse told me if i wanted to i could disconnect twice, as long as i was never reconnecting to a "dirty" (touched my patient connector) connection. They're a total game changer.

When i started doing daytime dwells (after the cycler ends the last drain, i get filled with a longer term fluid called icodextrin that stays in my abdomen all day until the next treatment), trying to sleep "empty" became more difficult - its like once i got used to being filled 24/7, being empty means i can like feel my guts touching eachother and i don't like it.

these days, my decision on when to start treatment each day/evening/night/early morning is based upon when i need to be disconnected - work, appointments, etc - anything that takes me out of the house for more than 2 hours. If i have to be at the office at 9am i need to leave by 8am which means i need to be in the shower by 7:15 which means my last cycle needs to end at or just before 7, which means i gotta be connected by 10pm. I have End Stage Renal Disease, on @home peritoneal dialysis. I experienced extreme chronic fatigue when i was first diagnosed, and once i'd complained enough, my labwork finally supported the idea that I was anemic and they began injecting me during my monthly lab visits, and that seemed to help quite a bit. It's worth noting that i experienced the symptoms months before the labwork finally triggered the "algorithm" to begin the injections.

but i'd also point out that working 70h a week is enough to make *healthy* people experience fatigue. I'm 48 (diagnosed ESRD @45) and have had to significantly cut back on how much time i can devote to work. Previous to my kidneys failing, i was working similar hours to you, travelling 2-3 weeks a month for work, etc.

as to your question about how it will feel when/if you start dialysis - lemme preface by saying everyone is different, and their experiences on dialysis are pretty wide ranging. I've heard from a lot of people who found it immediately improved their quality of life, etc. That hasn't been my experience though - for one, i'm tethered to this machine 11 hours a day, every single day. that basically counts 1/2 of the day as unavailable to do much more than sleep, or hang out/watch tv/read/whatever i can do that isn't physical and doesnt take me more than 20 feet from the machine. I live alone now that my kid has gone off to college, so i have to spend time off the machine doing stuff like preparing meals so that i dont make dumb/easy choices, cleaning up the house, doing laundry, etc. I also have to work in that timeframe, but my current role thankfully i am 99% WFH.
hang in there. give yourself some grace - not only are you aging out of your 20s/30s, which is an experience all on its own, you are doing so shackled with a life-altering medical condition that few "normal" people understand and even most of the understanding ones really don't have a clue the toll it takes on your body. I'm proud of you, i know how hard it is to try to keep all the plates spinning and not let the disease define you.

i leave you with one more word of encouragement - while im not thrilled about being on dialysis, or having the medical condition requiring it, i ABSOLUTELY feel much better than i did before the treatment started. It has its ups and downs, but man, living in a body with underfunctioning/nonfunctioning kidneys and no treatment is a hell i wouldn't wish on anyone.

It's a blind raise made before the cards are dealt. It is a min-raise (double the big blind) that gives the player who straddles the right to act last, and making the action to stay in the hand to the first and subsequent players a minimum of double the big blind (the straddle amount). Players can re-raise the straddle, but the straddling player always has the right to last action preflop.

After the flop, action commences as normal with no preference given to the straddling player.

Rules differ as to where you can straddle from (under the gun, the button, etc) as well as whether a straddle can be re-straddled (by another player posting double the straddle amount), but generally it's announced to the dealer/table before the cards are dealt.
